event_overview.title: About Gaza Peace Deal
event_overview.subject: Gaza Peace Deal
event_overview.summary: The Gaza peace deal is the name used for a U.S.-backed roadmap to implement a broader Gaza ceasefire and post-conflict transition. It links the decommissioning of weapons held by Hamas and other armed factions to a phased Israeli withdrawal, temporary international stabilization measures, Palestinian civilian administration, and reconstruction; its implementation remained conditional on verification and further agreed timetables as of August 22, 2026.

facts.label: Public roadmap
facts.value: A text published on July 31, 2026 described the arrangement as “A Roadmap for Completing the Implementation of President Trump’s Comprehensive Peace Plan in Gaza,” framed alongside UN Security Council Resolution 2803 (2025).

facts.label: Geographic and policy scope
facts.value: The roadmap concerns the Gaza Strip and states goals including ending hostilities, restoring civilian life, enabling Palestinian governance, supporting recovery and reconstruction, and creating conditions for Palestinian self-determination and statehood.

facts.label: Civil administration
facts.value: The proposed transitional civilian authority is the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), which the roadmap assigns responsibility for public services and, ultimately, control and storage of weapons in Gaza.

facts.label: Security and verification structure
facts.value: The roadmap calls for an International Verification Committee established by the Board of Peace to certify compliance before advancing phases. It also envisages a temporary International Stabilization Force to monitor the ceasefire, support humanitarian deliveries, train Palestinian police, and separate Israeli forces from NCAG-controlled areas.

facts.label: Sequencing
facts.value: Under the published text, weapons, military sites, depots, and tunnels would be decommissioned through a gradual, verified process connected to phased Israeli withdrawal; the timetable and operating mechanisms were to be prepared after approval of the roadmap rather than fixed in the text itself.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers late-July through mid-August 2026 announcements, responses, and related military developments around this roadmap; it does not attempt to cover the full Gaza war, all prior ceasefire diplomacy, or every stage of implementation.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War refers to the 2026 armed conflict involving the United States and Iran, with Israel participating in the initial strikes on Iran and Iran carrying out subsequent attacks across the region. The conflict has centered on military escalation, Iran’s nuclear program, regional security, and disruption of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, alongside intermittent ceasefire and mediation efforts.

facts.label: Start of major hostilities
facts.value: The United Nations said major hostilities began on February 28, 2026, when the United States and Israel carried out military strikes against Iran; Iran subsequently launched attacks affecting several neighboring states.

facts.label: Main parties and regional dimension
facts.value: The conflict principally involves the United States and Iran, while Israel was involved in the opening strikes and the effects have extended to Gulf states and maritime routes; the United Nations has described it as an international armed conflict.

facts.label: Strategic geography
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz—between Iran to the north and Oman and the United Arab Emirates to the south—has been a central flashpoint because of its importance to commercial shipping and regional energy trade.

facts.label: International legal and diplomatic conte
facts.value: UN Security Council resolution 2817 (2026) condemned actions or threats obstructing international navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and called for compliance with international law; the parties have also pursued ceasefire-related arrangements and indirect talks, including Qatar-facilitated discussions.

facts.label: Status by late July 2026
facts.value: The conflict had not reached a durable settlement: the United Nations reported continuing risks to shipping and wider escalation, while the United States publicly maintained military pressure and said it remained open to an agreement with Iran.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline focuses on late-July 2026 escalation, war-powers debate, maritime and oil-market effects, Houthi-related attacks, and ceasefire diplomacy; it does not provide a complete military, humanitarian, legal, or diplomatic history of the war.

event_overview.subject: Israeli-Palestinian Conflict
event_overview.summary: This event concerns lethal violence in the occupied West Bank involving Palestinians, Israeli settlers and, in some incidents, Israeli security forces. It occurs within the broader Israeli-Palestinian conflict, where settlement expansion, access to land, security operations and retaliatory attacks have long made rural communities and roads flashpoints.

facts.label: Location and status
facts.value: The West Bank, including East Jerusalem, is part of the Palestinian territory occupied by Israel since 1967 in the terminology used by the United Nations and the International Court of Justice.

facts.label: Governance framework
facts.value: The 1995 Israeli-Palestinian Interim Agreement (Oslo II) set interim arrangements for Palestinian self-government, security, elections and administration in the West Bank and Gaza pending a permanent-status settlement; it was designed as a five-year interim framework, not a final peace agreement.

facts.label: Settlement legal context
facts.value: UN Security Council Resolution 2334 states that Israeli settlements in Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem, have no legal validity and are a violation of international law. In its July 19, 2024 advisory opinion, the ICJ found that Israel’s transfer and maintenance of settlers in the West Bank and East Jerusalem is contrary to Article 49(6) of the Fourth Geneva Convention.

facts.label: Violence pattern
facts.value: UN OCHA defines settler-related violence broadly as violence, intimidation or trespass carried out by or against Israeli settlers and other Israeli civilians in the West Bank. Its incident classification distinguishes attacks by the identity of the initiator and can include alleged settler perpetrators, Israeli forces intervening in such incidents, Palestinian civilians and other actors.

facts.label: Protection and accountability context
facts.value: The ICJ’s 2024 advisory opinion found that settler violence against Palestinians, ineffective prevention or punishment of it, and excessive force can contribute to a coercive environment; this is a legal finding of the Court concerning Israel’s international obligations, rather than a determination of responsibility for any one incident.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows a limited sequence of reported violence, arrests, alleged arson, prosecutions, demolitions and sieges in late July and early August 2026; it does not provide a comprehensive history of the conflict, a complete casualty record, or final legal findings for each incident.

event_overview.title: About US-Canada Trade Relations
event_overview.subject: US-Canada Trade Relations
event_overview.summary: U.S.-Canada trade relations are a large, highly integrated bilateral economic relationship governed principally through the trilateral Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), called USMCA in the United States. The event concerns renewed friction over tariffs and market access within that broader relationship, including negotiations and reciprocal trade measures that can affect sectors and cross-border supply chains.

facts.label: Core trade framework
facts.value: Canada, the United States and Mexico are the three parties to CUSMA/USMCA, which replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA).

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: The agreement was signed on November 30, 2018, and entered into force on July 1, 2020; NAFTA had entered into force on January 1, 1994.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: CUSMA/USMCA sets rules for North American trade and investment, including goods market access and rules of origin, as well as provisions on digital trade, intellectual property, financial services, labor, environment and small and medium-sized enterprises.

facts.label: Dispute-resolution structure
facts.value: The agreement includes state-to-state dispute settlement under Chapter 31; USTR says its procedures were designed to prevent a party from blocking the formation of a panel, a problem under NAFTA.

facts.label: Scheduled review
facts.value: CUSMA/USMCA provides for a joint review every six years; Canada identifies July 1, 2026 as the date of the first review.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline follows the selected 2026 escalation in U.S.-Canada tariff talks and Canada’s stated response, but does not attempt to catalog the full history of bilateral trade, all CUSMA disputes, or every tariff measure affecting the two countries.

event_overview.title: About South Carolina Senate
event_overview.subject: South Carolina Senate
event_overview.summary: This is the South Carolina Republican Party’s emergency nomination process for the U.S. Senate race after Senator Lindsey Graham, the party’s 2026 nominee, died on July 11, 2026. It is distinct from a special election to fill the Senate vacancy: Darline Graham was appointed to serve temporarily, while the August primary and runoff select the Republican nominee for the statewide general-election ballot on November 3, 2026.

facts.label: Trigger and vacancy
facts.value: Lindsey Graham’s Senate service ended with his death on July 11, 2026; Darline Graham was appointed on July 13 and sworn in on July 14 to fill the resulting vacancy.

facts.label: Election purpose
facts.value: The South Carolina Election Commission said the special Republican filing period and primary were held under S.C. Code § 7-11-55 because the Republican U.S. Senate nominee died after facing general-election opposition; the resulting nominee will appear on the November 3, 2026 ballot.

facts.label: Dates and format
facts.value: The statewide special Republican primary was August 11, 2026, with a runoff scheduled for August 25 if no candidate won the nomination outright; early voting for the runoff was August 19–21.

facts.label: Administration and electorate
facts.value: The contest is statewide and administered by the South Carolina Election Commission and county election officials. Voters who participated in the June Republican primary, or did not vote in either June party primary, could vote; June Democratic-primary voters could not.

facts.label: Vacancy law
facts.value: Under South Carolina law, a gubernatorial Senate appointment generally lasts until January 3 after the next general election, and the governor must order an election connected to that general election if an unexpired term remains.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the August 2026 Republican nomination contest and related campaigning; it does not provide a complete account of the November general election, all candidates, or the full Senate vacancy process.

event_overview.title: About Immigration Policy
event_overview.subject: Immigration Policy
event_overview.summary: This event concerns U.S. immigration policy affecting noncitizens’ permission to remain, work, seek protection, or be removed from the United States. It centers on actions by the Department of Homeland Security and its components, immigration-court processes administered by the Justice Department, and litigation that can determine whether particular policies take effect.

facts.label: Governing framework
facts.value: The Immigration and Nationality Act authorizes the Secretary of Homeland Security to designate countries for Temporary Protected Status (TPS) when statutory country-condition criteria are met; TPS is a temporary benefit, not a path by itself to lawful permanent residence.

facts.label: Haiti TPS history and 2026 status
facts.value: Haiti was first designated for TPS on January 21, 2010. DHS announced a termination effective February 3, 2026; after court litigation, the U.S. Supreme Court reversed the lower-court stay on June 25, 2026, and the District Court acknowledged on August 5 that the stay was no longer in effect.

facts.label: Effect on individual immigration status
facts.value: A TPS termination does not by itself resolve every person’s immigration position: the federal notice says beneficiaries may return to a prior or other independently obtained valid status, if any, while separate removal or protection proceedings can also apply.

facts.label: Enforcement and adjudication roles
facts.value: ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations handles identification, arrest, detention, case management, and removals. Formal removal proceedings begin when DHS files a Notice to Appear with an immigration court; immigration judges determine removability and may decide applications for relief.

facts.label: Protection claims and visas
facts.value: Asylum is relief from removal for qualifying people who meet the refugee definition, whereas visas are travel documents and categories defined by immigration law and the purpose of travel. These are distinct legal mechanisms from TPS, though an individual’s case can involve more than one form of immigration status or protection.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline highlights major U.S. enforcement, detention, deportation, TPS, asylum, and visa-policy developments through August 25, 2026; it does not provide a complete account of every policy change, lawsuit, or individual immigration case.

event_overview.title: About Iran Sanctions
event_overview.subject: Iran Sanctions
event_overview.summary: Iran sanctions are a set of U.S. and international restrictive measures directed at Iranian government bodies, companies, individuals, and specified economic activity. In the United States, the measures combine statutes, presidential executive orders, and Treasury regulations; they are used in connection with concerns including nuclear proliferation, terrorism, missile activity, human-rights abuses, and sanctions evasion, while some humanitarian trade remains authorized or licensable.

facts.label: U.S. administration and legal framework
facts.value: The U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) administers the Iran sanctions program. OFAC says it implements multiple legal authorities, including executive orders, congressional statutes, regulations in 31 CFR Parts 535, 560, 561 and 562, and—in relevant cases—UN Security Council resolutions.

facts.label: Core U.S. trade restrictions
facts.value: The Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations, 31 CFR Part 560, contain prohibitions affecting imports, exports or reexports, trade-related dealings, investment, facilitation by U.S. persons, and transactions involving blocked property, subject to stated exceptions and licenses.

facts.label: Historical baseline
facts.value: A U.S. import embargo on Iranian-origin goods and services was imposed by Executive Order 12613 on October 29, 1987; comprehensive U.S. trade and financial sanctions followed in 1995 under Executive Order 12959. The present framework has subsequently been expanded and amended through further statutory and executive authorities.

facts.label: Humanitarian channels
facts.value: Sanctions do not amount to a blanket ban on humanitarian goods: OFAC maintains authorizations and licensing processes for agricultural commodities, medicine and medical devices, though restrictions can still apply where transactions involve designated parties or other prohibited activity.

facts.label: UN nuclear-related measures
facts.value: At the UN level, Security Council resolution 2231 of July 20, 2015 endorsed the JCPOA and replaced earlier Iran nuclear-related measures. The Security Council states that, effective September 27, 2025, the earlier resolutions’ provisions were reapplied through the resolution 2231 process and the 1737 sanctions list was re-established.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the August 23–24, 2026 U.S.-Iran sanctions-threat escalation and stated retaliation risks; it does not attempt to catalog the full history of every designation, legal authority, exemption, or diplomatic dispute.

event_overview.title: About Presidential Authority
event_overview.subject: Presidential Authority
event_overview.summary: This event is a legal dispute over whether the executive branch may demolish and replace the White House East Wing with a large ballroom without additional congressional authorization and preservation or environmental review. It centers on the limits of presidential authority over federally owned White House property, while also involving asserted security needs and historic-preservation concerns.

facts.label: Project and location
facts.value: The proposed White House Ballroom is planned for the former East Wing site in Washington, D.C. The White House described it as a roughly 90,000-square-foot event space with seating for about 650 people, intended to expand capacity for major official functions.

facts.label: Project timeline
facts.value: The White House announced the project on July 31, 2025 and initially said construction would begin in September 2025. A federal district-court opinion records that President Trump announced ground-breaking on October 20, 2025 and that the East Wing was subsequently demolished.

facts.label: Parties and claims
facts.value: The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued federal officials and the President on December 12, 2025. Its claims included alleged failures to undertake required consultation and NEPA review and to obtain congressional authorization; the litigation also raised constitutional separation-of-powers and federal-property questions.

facts.label: Core legal issue
facts.value: A central issue is whether existing statutes authorize the President and executive-branch entities to alter White House grounds and structures. The district-court record identifies 40 U.S.C. § 8106, concerning construction on public grounds in the District of Columbia without congressional authorization, among the provisions contested by the parties.

facts.label: Supreme Court emergency review
facts.value: In National Park Service v. National Trust for Historic Preservation, No. 26A203, the government filed an emergency application on August 13, 2026 seeking a stay of the construction injunction pending a planned certiorari petition. The Supreme Court docket lists the National Park Service and related federal entities as applicants and the National Trust as respondent.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the August 2026 injunction, appellate and emergency Supreme Court actions concerning construction, rather than the project’s full design, financing, preservation-review, or legislative history.

event_overview.title: About Ukraine Politics
event_overview.subject: Ukraine Politics
event_overview.summary: This event concerns Ukraine’s debate over whether to hold presidential, parliamentary or local elections while the country remains under martial law during Russia’s full-scale invasion. The issue combines legal restrictions on voting with practical questions about security, occupied territory, military service and the ability of displaced citizens to participate.

facts.label: Martial-law start
facts.value: Ukraine imposed martial law nationwide beginning at 5:30 a.m. on February 24, 2022, citing Russia’s military aggression; the Verkhovna Rada approved the presidential decree.

facts.label: Legal restriction on elections
facts.value: Ukraine’s Law on the Legal Regime of Martial Law bars presidential, parliamentary and local elections, as well as national and local referendums, during martial law.

facts.label: Constitutional continuity
facts.value: If the Verkhovna Rada’s term expires during martial law, its authority continues until the first sitting of a newly elected parliament after martial law is lifted; the legal framework also provides continuity for the presidency until a successor takes office.

facts.label: Election administration
facts.value: Ukraine’s Central Election Commission suspended electoral processes after martial law was introduced on February 24, 2022; post-martial-law election planning must address the resumption and scheduling of elections.

facts.label: Core practical constraints
facts.value: Official post-war election analysis identifies security conditions, occupied or recently liberated areas, population displacement, voter registration and election-administration capacity as major issues for any eventual nationwide vote.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the August 19–24, 2026 political debate over wartime elections and related scrutiny of Ukraine’s leadership, not the full history of Ukraine’s electoral system, martial law, corruption cases or the war.

event_overview.title: About Congo Ebola Outbreak
event_overview.subject: Congo Ebola Outbreak
event_overview.summary: The 2026 Congo Ebola outbreak is an ongoing epidemic of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), first declared by the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda on May 15, 2026. It is centered in eastern DR Congo, where transmission expanded rapidly amid conflict, population movement, and limits on health-system access; WHO has classified the event as a Public Health Emergency of International Concern.

facts.label: Start and status
facts.value: The health ministries of DR Congo and Uganda declared outbreaks of Bundibugyo virus disease on May 15, 2026. As of August 21, 2026, the outbreak remained active in DR Congo; Uganda had declared its outbreak over on July 28 after 42 days without a new locally transmitted case.

facts.label: Disease agent
facts.value: The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a species that causes Ebola disease. WHO reported that no licensed Bundibugyo-virus-specific vaccine or therapeutic was available, although candidate countermeasures were being developed and assessed.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: The epidemic began in Ituri Province and had spread to six DR Congo provinces by August 13: Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo, and an additional province reported in WHO's August risk assessment. Ituri remained the epicentre.

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: WHO's August 20 risk assessment reported 4,566 confirmed cases and 2,128 deaths in DR Congo as of August 13, 2026. Reported totals can change through delayed reporting, expanded testing, and reconciliation of earlier records.

facts.label: International framework and response
facts.value: On May 17, 2026, the WHO Director-General determined that the DR Congo–Uganda event constituted a Public Health Emergency of International Concern under the International Health Regulations. The response centers on surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, clinical care, community engagement, and cross-border preparedness.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline highlights major developments from July 22 through August 11, 2026; it does not provide a complete case ledger, every local response measure, or all cross-border and international updates.

event_overview.title: About Ceuta Border Surge
event_overview.subject: Ceuta Border Surge
event_overview.summary: The Ceuta Border Surge refers to a large-scale episode of irregular entries into Ceuta, Spain’s autonomous city on the Moroccan border, beginning on July 30, 2026. It prompted a joint Spanish-Moroccan border response, returns of people who entered irregularly, and emergency measures at the Tarajal breakwater; it also unfolded amid a court-related change in how Spain could apply its border-rejection regime to people arriving by swimming.

facts.label: Location and status
facts.value: Ceuta is an autonomous Spanish city; its land boundary with Morocco is an external border of the Schengen area.

facts.label: Event start
facts.value: Spain’s Interior Ministry identified July 30, 2026, as the day the migration crisis affected Ceuta and said Spain and Morocco had agreed to reinforce coordination and seek the rapid handover of people who entered illegally.

facts.label: Border-management authority
facts.value: External-border control is principally the responsibility of Spain as the EU member state concerned, under the Schengen Borders Code; the European Commission has described Ceuta and Melilla’s Moroccan borders as Schengen external borders.

facts.label: Spanish legal framework
facts.value: Spain’s Aliens Act provides a special Ceuta-and-Melilla regime allowing rejection at the border for people detected while overcoming border-containment elements, while requiring compliance with international human-rights and international-protection rules and providing for asylum applications at designated border-crossing locations.

facts.label: Immediate operational context
facts.value: On August 1, Spain’s Interior Ministry said it was installing a pneumatic barrier and containment buoys at the Tarajal breakwater after a July 8 Supreme Court ruling that the statutory rejection-at-the-border provision could not be applied to people who reached Ceuta by swimming where no physical containment element prevented access.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the acute surge and official response from July 30 through August 3, 2026; it does not attempt to document all later legal, humanitarian, diplomatic, or migration developments involving Ceuta and Morocco.

event_overview.title: About Iran Relations
event_overview.subject: Iran Relations
event_overview.summary: Iran relations in this timeline refers primarily to the adversarial relationship between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran, where military deterrence, diplomatic contacts, nuclear non-proliferation, sanctions, regional security and maritime transit can interact. The selected developments concern a period in which reported efforts to negotiate or pressure Iran are being weighed alongside threats of force and economic measures affecting Iran and third countries.

facts.label: Diplomatic status
facts.value: The United States and Iran severed diplomatic relations on April 7, 1980, following the November 4, 1979 seizure of the U.S. Embassy in Tehran; the two countries still have no formal diplomatic relationship. Switzerland has served as the U.S. protecting power in Iran since 1980.

facts.label: Sanctions framework
facts.value: U.S. economic restrictions concerning Iran are administered through a combination of statutes, presidential executive orders and Treasury regulations. OFAC describes the program as drawing on authorities including the Iran Sanctions Act, CISADA, CAATSA, IEEPA and regulations in 31 CFR Parts 535, 560, 561 and 562; general licenses can authorize specified activity otherwise prohibited.

facts.label: Nuclear diplomacy
facts.value: The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) was concluded on July 14, 2015 by Iran, China, France, Germany, Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States and the European Union, and was endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2231 on July 20, 2015. The UN states that, effective September 27, 2025, earlier Iran-related Security Council resolutions were re-applied under Resolution 2231's process.

facts.label: International nuclear safeguards
facts.value: Iran's safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency in connection with the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty entered into force on May 15, 1974. The IAEA lists an Additional Protocol signed by Iran on December 18, 2003, separately from the safeguards agreement.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the immediate diplomacy, coercive economic measures and regional trade or maritime pressures associated with this episode; it does not attempt to cover the full history of U.S.-Iran relations, every sanctions action, or all nuclear and regional-security developments.

event_overview.title: About the Eurovision Song Contest
event_overview.subject: Eurovision Song Contest
event_overview.summary: The Eurovision Song Contest is an annual international live music competition in which participating public-service broadcasters select performers and songs to represent them. It is organized under the auspices of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) and combines live televised performances with a competitive voting process to determine a winner.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: The first Contest was held in Switzerland on May 24, 1956, with seven participating nations.

facts.label: Governing framework
facts.value: The Contest is an international co-production by EBU Members, carried out under the auspices of the European Broadcasting Union as part of the Eurovision television-programme exchange.

facts.label: Participation model
facts.value: Participating public-service broadcasters—not national governments directly—enter artists and songs; in the 2026 edition, 35 broadcasters were confirmed as competitors.

facts.label: Competition format
facts.value: The modern Contest normally uses two Semi-Finals and a Grand Final; countries that qualify from the Semi-Finals join the previous year’s winner and the ‘Big Five’ broadcasters in the Final.

facts.label: 2027 edition
facts.value: The 71st Eurovision Song Contest is scheduled for Burgas, Bulgaria, at Arena Burgas, with Semi-Finals on May 11 and May 13, 2027, and the Grand Final on May 15; it will be hosted by Bulgarian National Television (BNT) with the EBU.

event_overview.title: About the 2026 FIFA World Cup
event_overview.subject: FIFA World Cup
event_overview.summary: The FIFA World Cup is FIFA’s flagship men’s national-team football competition, held in four-year cycles and bringing together teams that qualify through their regional confederations. The 2026 edition was staged jointly by Canada, Mexico and the United States and expanded the finals field from 32 to 48 teams, making it the largest edition of the tournament to date.

facts.label: Governing body
facts.value: The competition is organized by the Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA), whose statutes govern FIFA competitions and the process for awarding World Cup hosting rights.

facts.label: Origins
facts.value: FIFA approved the launch of the World Cup at its 1928 Congress, and the first tournament was held in Uruguay in 1930 with 13 participating teams.

facts.label: 2026 dates and hosts
facts.value: The 2026 FIFA World Cup ran from June 11 to July 19, 2026, across Canada, Mexico and the United States; it was the first World Cup co-hosted by three countries.

facts.label: Scale and format
facts.value: The 2026 finals featured 48 national teams, 104 matches and 12 groups of four. The top two teams in each group plus the eight best third-placed teams advanced to a round of 32, followed by single-elimination rounds.

facts.label: Host footprint
facts.value: Matches were assigned to 16 host cities: two in Canada, three in Mexico and 11 in the United States.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a late-July and early-August 2026 debate over proposed World Cup investment or equity arrangements and reactions from FIFA and UEFA; it does not aim to document the tournament’s matches, results, or the full history of FIFA governance and commercial operations.

event_overview.summary: A tourist helicopter crashed near Mount Ololokwe in Samburu County, northern Kenya, on August 19, 2026, killing all seven people aboard. The victims included Ecuadorian intelligence chief Michele Sensi-Contugi and his wife, along with five U.S. citizens; Kenyan aviation authorities were investigating the cause, which had not been publicly established as of August 20.

facts.label: Date
facts.value: The crash occurred on the morning of August 19, 2026; initial reports placed it at about 9:13 a.m. local time.

facts.label: Location and route
facts.value: The helicopter went down near Mount Ololokwe in Samburu County after departing the Loisaba area for Ewaso Nyiro in northern Kenya.

facts.label: People aboard
facts.value: There were seven people aboard: a pilot and six passengers. Reporting and government confirmations identified the dead as Michele Sensi-Contugi, director general of Ecuador's intelligence agency, his wife, and five U.S. citizens.

facts.label: Aircraft
facts.value: The aircraft was reported as a Eurocopter EC130 B4, registered in Kenya as 5Y-GYM.

facts.label: Investigation status
facts.value: The cause had not been determined publicly by August 20; Kenya's civil-aviation authorities were conducting an investigation.

event_overview.title: About Children's Privacy Lawsuit
event_overview.subject: Children's Privacy Lawsuit
event_overview.summary: This event concerns a U.S. civil children’s-privacy case in which the Department of Justice, acting after a Federal Trade Commission referral, alleged that TikTok and ByteDance violated the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). The litigation ended in an announced August 2026 settlement; the government stated that the claims were allegations and that there had been no determination of liability.

facts.label: Case timeline
facts.value: The United States filed the lawsuit on August 2, 2024; the Justice Department announced the settlement on August 21, 2026.

facts.label: Parties and forum
facts.value: The case was brought by the United States against ByteDance, TikTok, and affiliated entities in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, Civil Action No. 2:24-cv-06535.

facts.label: Legal scope
facts.value: The case concerned COPPA and its implementing rule, which generally require online services to give notice to and obtain parental consent before knowingly collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children under 13; the government also alleged noncompliance with a prior order involving TikTok’s predecessor, Musical.ly.

facts.label: Government allegations
facts.value: The 2024 complaint alleged that TikTok allowed children under 13 to use regular accounts, collected and retained their personal information without required parental notice or consent, and often failed to honor parents’ requests to delete accounts and data.

facts.label: Settlement structure
facts.value: According to the Justice Department, TikTok is to pay $300 million immediately and a further $100 million if a court enters an order vacating the earlier Musical.ly consent decree; DOJ described the resolution as one of the largest recoveries in a COPPA case.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the August 2026 settlement news, not the full history of COPPA enforcement against TikTok/Musical.ly or other children’s-privacy litigation.

event_overview.title: About Russia-Ukraine War
event_overview.subject: Russia-Ukraine War
event_overview.summary: The Russia-Ukraine War is an ongoing armed conflict between Ukraine and the Russian Federation, rooted in fighting that began in eastern Ukraine in 2014 and greatly escalated with Russia’s full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022. It has involved conventional ground operations as well as long-range missile and drone attacks, and has produced a major humanitarian and displacement crisis.

facts.label: Origins and escalation
facts.value: Conflict-related humanitarian operations in eastern Ukraine expanded in 2014; Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022 transformed the conflict into a nationwide emergency.

facts.label: Main parties and geography
facts.value: The war principally involves Ukraine and the Russian Federation, with military operations taking place in Ukraine and attacks increasingly affecting areas beyond the immediate front line.

facts.label: International legal position
facts.value: On March 2, 2022, the UN General Assembly deplored Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, demanded that Russia end its use of force and withdraw its forces, and reaffirmed Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognized borders.

facts.label: International Court of Justice proceedin
facts.value: In provisional measures issued on March 16, 2022 in Ukraine v. Russian Federation, the International Court of Justice ordered Russia to suspend military operations begun on February 24, 2022, while stating that the order did not decide the case’s merits.

facts.label: Humanitarian impact
facts.value: The war has driven large-scale displacement, damaged civilian infrastructure and left millions of people in need of assistance; UNHCR describes it as an ongoing full-scale war and humanitarian emergency.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline focuses on specified late-July and early-August 2026 security developments, including cross-border drone or missile incidents and strikes; it does not aim to provide a complete account of the war’s military, diplomatic, legal, or humanitarian history.

event_overview.title: About Gaza Conflict
event_overview.subject: Gaza Conflict
event_overview.summary: The Gaza conflict refers to the war centered on the Gaza Strip that followed Hamas-led attacks in Israel on October 7, 2023, and Israel’s subsequent military campaign against Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups. It combines active hostilities, hostage and detainee issues, humanitarian access and civilian protection concerns, ceasefire diplomacy, and international legal and accountability processes.

facts.label: Start and setting
facts.value: The current phase began on October 7, 2023, when Palestinian armed groups from Gaza carried out attacks in Israel; the ensuing Israeli military campaign has been focused principally on the Gaza Strip.

facts.label: Principal parties
facts.value: The conflict principally involves Israel and Hamas, alongside other Palestinian armed groups; civilians in Gaza and Israel have been affected by the hostilities.

facts.label: Humanitarian dimension
facts.value: UN humanitarian reporting describes continuing military activity, displacement, damage to civilian infrastructure, and constraints on access to health care, water, sanitation, shelter, and essential supplies in Gaza.

facts.label: Ceasefire and hostage diplomacy
facts.value: A UN Security Council resolution adopted on June 10, 2024 endorsed a proposed three-phase framework linking a ceasefire, releases of hostages and Palestinian prisoners, Israeli force withdrawals, humanitarian aid, and reconstruction; implementation has depended on agreement by the parties.

facts.label: International legal process
facts.value: The International Court of Justice is hearing South Africa’s case against Israel under the Genocide Convention and has issued orders on provisional measures; those measures are interim directions and do not determine the case’s final merits.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows selected August 2026 developments involving strikes, ceasefire and disarmament diplomacy, and investigations into particular killings; it does not provide a comprehensive record of the war, all casualties, or every diplomatic and legal development.

event_overview.title: About Wildfires
event_overview.subject: Wildfires
event_overview.summary: This event is a news timeline about a cluster of wildfire emergencies in Europe in late July and early August 2026, initially centered on France and Spain and later including Greece. It concerns the civil-protection consequences of fast-moving vegetation fires, including evacuation orders, firefighting operations, damage assessments and, where applicable, investigations into suspected human causes.

facts.label: Timeline period
facts.value: The selected timeline runs from July 25 through August 7, 2026; its France-and-Spain-focused entries precede later entries concerning wildfire emergencies in Greece.

facts.label: European monitoring
facts.value: The European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS), operated through the EU's Copernicus Emergency Management Service and the Joint Research Centre, provides Europe-wide fire-danger forecasts and information on active fires, burned area and fire impacts. EFFIS figures can differ from national reports because its mapped-fire methodology and thresholds differ.

facts.label: France response framework
facts.value: In France, wildfire response emphasizes early detection and deployment of appropriate resources, alongside prevention measures such as vegetation clearance around exposed buildings and restrictions on burning or forest access during high-risk periods.

facts.label: Spain response framework
facts.value: Spain's autonomous communities are responsible for wildfire defense, while the national government coordinates core activities, provides state firefighting support and compiles the national wildfire statistics. The official EGIF system records standardized information from wildfire reports submitted by the autonomous communities.

facts.label: EU mutual assistance
facts.value: When national capacity is strained, the EU Civil Protection Mechanism can coordinate cross-border assistance; its rescEU reserve includes firefighting aircraft and helicopters, while the Emergency Response Coordination Centre monitors risks and emergencies across Europe.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows major reported evacuation, response and alleged-arson developments linked to the late-July 2026 fires in France, Spain and Greece; it does not attempt to catalog every wildfire, establish final burned-area or displacement totals, or replace official national incident records.

event_overview.title: About Ukraine Conflict
event_overview.subject: Ukraine Conflict
event_overview.summary: The Ukraine conflict is the ongoing interstate war centered on Russia’s military actions against Ukraine, including the full-scale invasion launched on February 24, 2022, against a backdrop of Russia’s actions in and against Ukraine since 2014. It has involved sustained combat, long-range missile and drone attacks, humanitarian disruption, and international diplomatic, legal, and sanctions responses.

facts.label: Conflict timeline
facts.value: Russia’s full-scale invasion began on February 24, 2022; international institutions also treat the wider situation as encompassing events in Ukraine from 2013-14 onward.

facts.label: Location and parties
facts.value: The conflict is fought primarily on and over Ukraine’s internationally recognized territory, involving Russia and Ukraine; the UN General Assembly has repeatedly reaffirmed Ukraine’s sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity within those borders.

facts.label: International legal position
facts.value: The UN General Assembly’s March 2, 2022 resolution characterized Russia’s actions as aggression against Ukraine and demanded that Russia end its use of force and withdraw its military forces.

facts.label: International criminal investigation
facts.value: The International Criminal Court opened its Ukraine investigation on March 2, 2022. Its stated scope covers alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide committed by any person on any part of Ukraine’s territory from November 21, 2013 onward.

facts.label: Humanitarian dimension
facts.value: The war has produced a major humanitarian and displacement emergency; UNHCR describes the February 2022 escalation as one of the fastest-growing displacement emergencies in recent history.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows major late-July and early-August 2026 military, diplomatic and cross-border developments connected to the war; it does not attempt to provide a complete account of the conflict’s battlefield, humanitarian, political or legal history.

event_overview.title: About Indonesia Earthquake
event_overview.subject: Indonesia Earthquake
event_overview.summary: “Indonesia Earthquake” is a rolling disaster-news topic covering significant earthquakes affecting Indonesia, rather than a single tournament, institution, or event with fixed dates. Indonesia’s seismic risk is driven by its position across active plate-boundary systems, so individual earthquakes can occur in different regions and may create tsunami concerns depending on their location, depth, and source mechanism.

facts.label: Geographic and tectonic setting
facts.value: Indonesia lies across complex active plate boundaries. Along Java and the Sunda Arc, the India-Australia plates converge with and subduct beneath the Sunda Plate; eastern Indonesia also involves convergent interactions among the Pacific, Australia, Philippine Sea, and Sunda plates.

facts.label: Nature of the topic
facts.value: The topic has no fixed start or end date, host, or participant list: it groups separate earthquake incidents in Indonesia and their humanitarian, infrastructure, and tsunami-related consequences.

facts.label: National monitoring authority
facts.value: Indonesia’s Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) performs government functions in meteorology, climatology, and geophysics; BMKG states that it is responsible for monitoring earthquakes in Indonesia.

facts.label: Warning framework
facts.value: BMKG operates the Indonesia Tsunami Early Warning System (InaTEWS) and is Indonesia’s national tsunami warning center. BMKG issues earthquake and tsunami information, while local governments and disaster-management bodies are responsible for disseminating and amplifying warnings to communities.

facts.label: Legal basis
facts.value: Law No. 31 of 2009 on Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics, enacted on October 1, 2009, is the governing legal framework listed by BMKG for this field.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline is intended to track the specified Indonesia-related earthquake development and its reported effects; it does not provide a complete record of all Indonesian earthquakes, aftershocks, historical disasters, or unrelated earthquakes elsewhere, including the Colombia item listed in the supplied timeline.

event_overview.title: About US-South Korea Relations
event_overview.subject: US-South Korea Relations
event_overview.summary: The developments concern a reported direction to reduce U.S.-Republic of Korea combined military training, a recurring element of the two countries’ security alliance. Any such change would affect exercises used to rehearse combined command, interoperability and responses to contingencies on the Korean Peninsula.

facts.label: Alliance basis
facts.value: The U.S.-ROK security relationship is grounded in the Mutual Defense Treaty signed on October 1, 1953; U.S. Forces Korea describes recent combined exercises as operating in the treaty’s spirit.

facts.label: Main exercise framework
facts.value: Freedom Shield and Ulchi Freedom Shield are annual combined exercises involving the Republic of Korea and the United States; Ulchi Freedom Shield is described by USFK as combined, joint, all-domain and interagency training.

facts.label: Participants and command structure
facts.value: USFK identifies the Combined Forces Command, U.S. Forces Korea, United Nations Command, the ROK Joint Chiefs of Staff and ROK government agencies as participants in Ulchi Freedom Shield. Freedom Shield is conducted under the Combined Forces Command.

facts.label: Format and stated purpose
facts.value: The exercises combine live, virtual, constructive and field-based training. USFK says their stated purposes include strengthening combined readiness, interoperability and the alliance’s ability to respond to security threats; it characterizes Freedom Shield as defensive in nature.

facts.label: Recent baseline
facts.value: Freedom Shield 26 ran from March 9 to March 19, 2026, and included Warrior Shield, field training across the Korean Peninsula involving ground, maritime, air and Marine forces.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the August 17-18, 2026 policy developments concerning reductions in joint exercises, not the full history of the U.S.-ROK alliance, all military training, or subsequent implementation details.

event_overview.title: About Central African Republic Mining
event_overview.subject: Central African Republic Mining
event_overview.summary: This event concerns the collapse of an artisanal gold-mining site in Zamboye, a village in the Central African Republic’s Nana-Mambéré prefecture near the Cameroon border, on August 18, 2026. Rescue operations and official efforts to establish the cause, operator responsibility, and final casualty count followed; early reporting described a death toll exceeding 100, though figures remained subject to confirmation.

facts.label: Incident date and place
facts.value: The collapse occurred on August 18, 2026, at a low-technology artisanal gold mine in Zamboye, Nana-Mambéré prefecture, near Cameroon.

facts.label: Mining method
facts.value: The affected operation was described as artisanal gold mining, the small-scale and largely manual form of extraction that accounts for much of the country’s gold and diamond production.

facts.label: Regulator and legal framework
facts.value: The Ministry of Mines and Geology oversees national mining policy; mining is governed by the 2024 Mining Code, Law No. 24-008.

facts.label: National sector context
facts.value: Gold and diamonds are the Central African Republic’s principal mineral commodities, but the sector remains substantially informal and has been associated with conflict and illicit trade risks.

facts.label: Why the event has wider significance
facts.value: Artisanal mining is an important source of income in mineral-producing communities: a World Bank project document estimated that roughly 600,000 Central Africans depended on the sector at least partly for income.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the immediate August 2026 collapse and ensuing mine-closure response, not the full history of Central African Republic mining, all artisanal-mining accidents, or the eventual investigation findings.

event_overview.title: About Syria Conflict
event_overview.subject: Syria Conflict
event_overview.summary: The Syria conflict began with anti-government protests in March 2011 and escalated into armed conflict involving Syrian state forces, opposition armed groups, extremist organizations and foreign actors. It has produced a major humanitarian and displacement crisis, while international efforts have combined diplomacy, humanitarian relief and mechanisms intended to support accountability for serious international crimes.

facts.label: Origin and location
facts.value: The conflict began in Syria in March 2011, after protests that started in Dar'a spread following the violent suppression of demonstrations.

facts.label: Political framework
facts.value: UN Security Council resolution 2254, adopted in 2015, remains the UN-backed framework cited for pursuing a Syrian-led, negotiated political settlement rather than a military solution.

facts.label: International accountability mechanism
facts.value: The UN General Assembly established the International, Impartial and Independent Mechanism (IIIM) on December 21, 2016, to assist investigations and prosecutions of those responsible for the most serious crimes under international law committed in Syria since March 2011.

facts.label: Legal scope
facts.value: The IIIM is not itself a court: it collects, consolidates, preserves and analyzes material and prepares case files for use by competent jurisdictions, subject to human-rights and fair-trial standards.

facts.label: Humanitarian and regional impact
facts.value: The conflict has displaced Syrians both within the country and across the region; UNHCR identifies Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon and Türkiye among the countries affected by the Syria emergency.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the specific reported court proceedings concerning Bashar al-Assad; it does not attempt to catalog the full military, political, humanitarian or accountability history of the Syria conflict.

event_overview.title: About Colombia Earthquake
event_overview.subject: Colombia Earthquake
event_overview.summary: The Colombia earthquake was a magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck western Colombia on August 10, 2026, causing major building damage and trapping people beneath collapsed structures. Pereira, in the coffee-growing region of Risaralda, was among the affected cities, and the event prompted a continuing search-and-rescue and disaster-response operation.

facts.label: Start date
facts.value: The main earthquake struck on August 10, 2026; rescue and damage-assessment operations continued in the following days.

facts.label: Magnitude and affected area
facts.value: The earthquake was reported as magnitude 7.4 and affected western Colombia, including Pereira, Cali, Quibdó and Manizales; it was also felt in Ecuador and Panama.

facts.label: Pereira’s setting
facts.value: Pereira is the capital of Risaralda department and the largest city in Colombia’s Eje Cafetero (Coffee Axis); it is located in central-western Colombia.

facts.label: Seismic monitoring
facts.value: The Servicio Geológico Colombiano (SGC) is the national geological authority that publishes earthquake information and seismic-hazard tools; its seismic catalog contains events from 1993 onward and says entries are manually reviewed by SGC seismology analysts.

facts.label: Response framework
facts.value: Colombia’s disaster-risk system is established under Law 1523 of 2012. The law assigns disaster-risk management to national and territorial authorities and gives the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) a coordinating role across the system.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the immediate rescue phase in Pereira on August 12-13, 2026, rather than providing a complete account of all affected places, casualty revisions, relief measures, or longer-term recovery.

event_overview.title: About Approache Hurricane Storm
event_overview.subject: Approache Hurricane Storm
event_overview.summary: Hurricane Lala was a Central Pacific tropical cyclone that developed in mid-August 2026 and threatened Hawaiʻi, particularly the Island of Hawaiʻi. The storm strengthened from a tropical storm into a Category 1 hurricane while producing hazardous wind, rain and surf conditions near the state.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: Lala formed as a tropical storm on August 13, 2026, and strengthened into a hurricane on August 15; the event was still unfolding as of August 16, 2026.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: The storm approached and passed near Hawaiʻi, with the Island of Hawaiʻi (the Big Island) facing the principal immediate threat; reporting on August 15 said its center skirted the island rather than making landfall.

facts.label: Intensity
facts.value: Lala reached Category 1 hurricane strength, with maximum sustained winds reported at 75 mph (120 km/h) on August 15.

facts.label: Forecast authority
facts.value: Tropical-cyclone outlooks and advisories for the Central Pacific, including the area around Hawaiʻi, are issued by the National Weather Service’s Central Pacific Hurricane Center in Honolulu in coordination with the National Hurricane Center.

facts.label: Naming and season
facts.value: Lala was listed as the first name in the 2026 Central Pacific tropical-cyclone naming sequence; the Central Pacific hurricane season runs from June 1 through November 30.

event_overview.scope_note: This timeline covers Lala’s approach to and effects on Hawaiʻi during August 15–16, 2026, not every advisory, local damage report, response action, or later stage of the storm.

event_overview.title: About Zambia Elections
event_overview.subject: Zambia Elections
event_overview.summary: Zambia’s 2026 general election is the nationwide vote to choose the President and other national and local officeholders. The presidential contest elects a President and Vice-President running mate; the outcome is determined under Zambia’s constitutional majoritarian system and administered by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ).

facts.label: Date and location
facts.value: The first ballot was held nationwide in Zambia on Thursday, August 13, 2026, the constitutionally scheduled second Thursday of August for a general election held every five years.

facts.label: Offices covered
facts.value: A Zambian general election combines elections for President, Members of Parliament, mayors, council chairpersons and councillors on the same day.

facts.label: Presidential voting system
facts.value: The President is elected directly by registered voters with a Vice-President as running mate. A candidate must receive more than 50% of valid votes; otherwise, the top two candidates proceed to a second ballot within 37 days.

facts.label: Election authority
facts.value: The ECZ is the constitutional electoral management body responsible for implementing the electoral process, conducting elections, registering voters, accrediting observers and agents, and regulating electoral conduct.

facts.label: Results process
facts.value: The ECZ’s revised roadmap scheduled receipt and verification of results for August 15–17, 2026, followed by declaration of results on August 17; this timetable describes the planned process rather than a final outcome.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows immediate developments around polling, counting and disruptions in the August 2026 presidential vote; it does not provide a complete account of all races, campaigns, legal challenges or final certified results.

event_overview.title: About Southwest France Wildfire
event_overview.subject: Southwest France Wildfire
event_overview.summary: The Southwest France wildfire was a major late-July 2026 forest-fire emergency in Gironde, west of Bordeaux, affecting the wooded Atlantic-coast area around Saumos and the Lège-Cap-Ferret peninsula. It prompted large-scale precautionary evacuations of residents and summer visitors, with French emergency services using both land and maritime routes to move people and secure affected areas.

facts.label: Start and location
facts.value: The fire began around July 22, 2026, in the forested Gironde area between Saumos and Lège-Cap-Ferret, north of the Arcachon Basin on France's Atlantic coast.

facts.label: Evacuation authority and operations
facts.value: The Gironde prefecture ordered the evacuation of the Cap Ferret peninsula; the response involved firefighters, the Gendarmerie nationale, and evacuation by road and sea.

facts.label: Scale of displacement
facts.value: Evacuation totals changed as the fire spread, but reporting documented more than 10,000 people moved to safety on July 23 and a full-peninsula evacuation as conditions worsened.

facts.label: Return phase
facts.value: By July 30, authorities had begun allowing people back to locations they judged safe, while firefighting and safety operations continued.

facts.label: Underlying local risk framework
facts.value: Lège-Cap-Ferret is officially designated as exposed to forest-fire risk; its state-prescribed forest-fire risk-prevention plan dates from October 1, 2004, and the commune is subject to mandatory vegetation-clearance requirements.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows major evacuation and wildfire developments connected to southwest France and related European fire coverage, but does not provide a complete incident log, final damage assessment, or definitive investigation findings.

event_overview.title: About Iran Threats
event_overview.subject: Iran Threats
event_overview.summary: This event concerns reported protective travel measures taken during President Donald Trump’s departure from the NATO summit in Ankara, Türkiye, on July 8, 2026. U.S. officials told news outlets that intelligence indicated a credible threat involving Iran and Iran-aligned proxy groups, leading to the reported use of a different presidential aircraft; the specific threat details have not been publicly documented by the U.S. government.

facts.label: Date and location
facts.value: The reported aircraft change occurred as Trump departed Ankara, Türkiye, after the July 7-8, 2026 NATO summit.

facts.label: Summit context
facts.value: Türkiye hosted the 2026 NATO summit at the Beştepe Presidential Compound in Ankara; NATO describes summits as meetings of Allied heads of state and government that provide strategic direction for the Alliance.

facts.label: Reported protective measure
facts.value: CBS News reported, citing U.S. officials, that Trump departed on the older Air Force One aircraft rather than the newer Qatar-donated plane after intelligence identified a credible threat to the president from Iran and allied proxy groups.

facts.label: Nature of the allegation
facts.value: The reporting characterized the intelligence as involving a possible missile attack on the president’s aircraft. This was an account attributed to unnamed officials, rather than a publicly released U.S. intelligence finding or criminal case.

facts.label: Protection responsibility
facts.value: The U.S. Secret Service’s protective mission includes ensuring the safety of the president, alongside other protected officials, visiting heads of state, and designated events.

event_overview.title: About Iran Conflict
event_overview.subject: Iran Conflict
event_overview.summary: The Iran Conflict refers here to the 2026 direct military confrontation between the United States and Iran, which has expanded beyond Iranian territory to include attacks and claimed attacks on U.S. forces, partner states and maritime activity in the Middle East. The confrontation has centered in part on control and security of the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran’s reported retaliatory operations have involved missiles and drones directed at regional sites hosting U.S. personnel.

facts.label: Start of the direct conflict
facts.value: Reporting describes U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, 2026, as the start of the present direct war; it is distinct from the longer-running U.S.-Iran rivalry and regional proxy conflicts.

facts.label: Ceasefire and renewed fighting
facts.value: The United States and Iran reached an interim arrangement or ceasefire in mid-June 2026, but reporting says the truce subsequently broke down amid a confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz and renewed U.S. and Iranian attacks.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: The conflict’s military and economic effects extend across Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and neighboring states that host U.S. facilities, including Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan; reports of individual strikes and damage may be contested or unverified.

facts.label: Why Bahrain and Kuwait matter
facts.value: Bahrain hosts U.S. Naval Support Activity Bahrain and the U.S. Fifth Fleet/NAVCENT presence, while Camp Arifjan in Kuwait supports Army prepositioned stocks and theater sustainment for U.S. Central Command operations.

facts.label: Maritime dimension
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz is a central theater because it is a strategic shipping chokepoint; the U.S. Fifth Fleet’s area of responsibility includes the Arabian Gulf and the strait, alongside other regional waterways.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline follows selected 2026 escalations involving U.S.-Iran military and maritime actions, including reported attacks affecting U.S. regional facilities, rather than documenting every diplomatic, proxy, domestic or historical aspect of U.S.-Iran relations.

event_overview.title: About Mountaineering Incident
event_overview.subject: Mountaineering Incident
event_overview.summary: This event is a fatal avalanche involving a 10-person mountaineering expedition on Broad Peak in Pakistan’s Karakoram range. The avalanche struck on July 30, 2026, during an ascent attempt; after search operations were constrained by severe conditions, the expedition company confirmed that all 10 climbers had died.

facts.label: Date and outcome
facts.value: The avalanche occurred on July 30, 2026. By August 1, the expedition company had confirmed the deaths of all 10 members of the group.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Broad Peak is an 8,047-metre mountain in the Karakoram on the Pakistan–China border, in the Gilgit-Baltistan region of Pakistan.

facts.label: Expedition
facts.value: The affected party was a 10-member climbing expedition attempting to summit Broad Peak; Nirmal Purja was identified in reporting as its leader.

facts.label: Search and recovery
facts.value: Rescuers initially located four bodies and recovered three, while harsh weather impeded helicopter-supported search and recovery operations.

facts.label: Protected-area context
facts.value: Broad Peak is among the mountains within Central Karakoram National Park, a Gilgit-Baltistan protected area established in 1993.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the initial reports of climbers missing, the reported death toll, and subsequent confirmation of all 10 deaths; it does not provide a complete account of recovery operations, the avalanche’s cause, or wider climbing-season developments.

event_overview.title: About Typhoon Dolphin
event_overview.subject: Typhoon Dolphin
event_overview.summary: Typhoon Dolphin was the 13th named tropical cyclone of the 2026 western North Pacific season, forming in late July and later tracking westward across the region. It affected Japan’s Okinawa area before making landfall in Zhejiang province on China’s east coast; by August 10 it had weakened to a tropical storm inland.

facts.label: Formation and designation
facts.value: China’s National Meteorological Center designated Dolphin as 2026’s No. 13 typhoon; official reporting said it formed over the northwestern Pacific on July 27, 2026.

facts.label: China landfall and weakening
facts.value: Dolphin made landfall near Taizhou, Zhejiang, on the evening of August 9 with reported winds of 151 kph; on August 10, China’s National Meteorological Center listed it as a tropical storm over Dexing, Jiangxi, and forecast further weakening.

facts.label: Naming system
facts.value: “Dolphin” is a name contributed by Hong Kong, China, under the ESCAP/WMO Typhoon Committee naming list; it refers to the Chinese white dolphin and a Hong Kong mascot.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the August 8-10 Japan-to-China impact period and preparedness or disruption measures, not Dolphin’s full late-July development, its complete inland dissipation, or all effects elsewhere in the region.

event_overview.title: About COVID-19 Hearing
event_overview.subject: COVID-19 Hearing
event_overview.summary: This was a U.S. Senate oversight hearing featuring former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases director Anthony Fauci, held by the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs (HSGAC). It occurred in the context of the committee’s continuing examination of federal handling of COVID-19 origins, related research, and government transparency; the selected timeline focuses on the immediate dispute over testimony and possible congressional enforcement rather than resolving the pandemic’s origin.

facts.label: Date and venue
facts.value: The full-committee hearing, listed as “Testimony of Anthony Fauci,” was held on July 29, 2026, at 8:30 a.m. in room SD-342 of the Senate Dirksen Building.

facts.label: Witness
facts.value: The hearing’s sole listed witness was Anthony Fauci, M.D., identified by the committee as former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, a position he held from 1984 to 2022, within the National Institutes of Health and Department of Health and Human Services.

facts.label: Subject context
facts.value: In a May 2026 HSGAC hearing on COVID-19 and gain-of-function research, the committee framed its inquiry around the origins of COVID-19, intelligence-community transparency, potential conflicts involving outside scientific advisers, and federal research oversight. Those are the surrounding issues for the later Fauci testimony, not findings established by the hearing itself.

facts.label: Congressional-enforcement framework
facts.value: Federal law provides that a person summoned by either chamber or a committee who willfully defaults or refuses to answer a question pertinent to the inquiry may face criminal contempt of Congress; under 2 U.S.C. § 194, a contempt matter may be certified to the appropriate U.S. attorney. Whether a particular assertion of the Fifth Amendment supports contempt is a fact- and law-specific question.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the July 29–31, 2026 testimony dispute and ensuing contempt discussion, not the full history of COVID-19 origins investigations, Fauci’s career, or all Senate pandemic hearings.

event_overview.title: About Japan Flooding
event_overview.subject: Japan Flooding
event_overview.summary: Japan Flooding refers to the heavy-rain emergency that began affecting eastern Japan on August 13, 2026, with the most severe reported impacts centered on Chiba Prefecture, east of Tokyo. Intense short-duration rainfall flooded roads and homes, disrupted transport and power service, and prompted warnings for both inundation and landslides; casualty figures remained subject to official confirmation as response operations continued.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: The event was reported as beginning on August 13, 2026; the selected timeline follows developments reported through August 15, 2026, rather than establishing a final end date.

facts.label: Primary area affected
facts.value: The acute flooding emergency was concentrated in Chiba Prefecture in eastern Japan, near Tokyo, although the broader weather system affected eastern Japan.

facts.label: Meteorological hazard
facts.value: The rainfall was characterized as record-breaking in parts of Chiba, with forecasts and reports of more than 100 millimeters of rain in an hour in Chiba City and nearby municipalities; the associated risks included urban flooding and landslides.

facts.label: Warnings and public-warning system
facts.value: The Japan Meteorological Agency issued its highest-level heavy-rain warning for 14 Chiba municipalities during the event. In Chiba, JMA weather warnings and advisories have been issued on a municipality-by-municipality basis since 2010.

facts.label: Reported human impact
facts.value: By August 14, reporting cited at least five deaths in Chiba after the rainfall and flooding. This was an early reported toll and may be revised as authorities verify cases.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the immediate August 14-15, 2026 flooding and fatality reports, not a complete accounting of all weather impacts, response measures, damage assessments, or later revisions to casualties.

event_overview.title: About Plagiarism Scandal
event_overview.subject: Plagiarism Scandal
event_overview.summary: This controversy concerns allegations about attribution and other claims in the academic record of Jason Arday, a sociologist who joined the University of Cambridge’s Faculty of Education in 2023. The issue drew renewed public attention in July and August 2026, when reporting described questions about his 2015 doctoral thesis and publications; Arday denied plagiarism, while Cambridge said it had opened an inquiry into new information concerning his qualifications and honorary appointments.

facts.label: Academic role and location
facts.value: Arday was appointed Professor of Sociology of Education in the University of Cambridge Faculty of Education, in Cambridge, England, with the appointment taking effect on March 6, 2023.

facts.label: Doctoral record
facts.value: Cambridge’s faculty profile listed Arday’s PhD in Education as awarded by Liverpool John Moores University; reporting said Cambridge had initially relied on Liverpool John Moores University’s prior consideration of plagiarism allegations concerning the doctorate.

facts.label: Publication corrections
facts.value: A December 6, 2023 correction to Arday’s 2018 Social Sciences article added citations and stated that overlap with earlier work had not been fully identified in the original text; the notice said the author maintained that the scientific conclusions were unaffected.

facts.label: Second correction
facts.value: A May 16, 2024 correction to a 2020 Educational Philosophy and Theory article clarified its relationship to Arday’s 2018 study and to a 2016 study by Memon and colleagues, adding citations in the methodology section.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers reactions and calls for reflection following Arday’s death on August 15–16, 2026; it does not attempt to resolve the allegations, determine the outcome of Cambridge’s inquiry, or catalogue every publication and claim at issue.

event_overview.title: About Women's Africa Cup of Nations
event_overview.subject: Women's Africa Cup of Nations
event_overview.summary: The Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) is the Confederation of African Football’s continental championship for African women’s senior national teams. Morocco 2026 is an expanded edition of the competition and also serves as CAF’s qualifying route for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: The official match schedule set the tournament from 26 July to 16 August 2026, with the final in Rabat on 16 August.

facts.label: Host and venues
facts.value: Morocco hosted the tournament, with matches scheduled in Rabat and Casablanca.

facts.label: Organizer
facts.value: The competition is organized by the Confederation of African Football (CAF), Africa’s football governing body, in conjunction with a local organizing committee for this edition.

facts.label: Participants and format
facts.value: Sixteen national teams competed for the first time, divided into four groups of four; the leading teams progressed to a knockout phase culminating in the final.

facts.label: World Cup qualification role
facts.value: The four WAFCON semi-finalists qualify directly for the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil, while the losing quarter-finalists play for two CAF places in the FIFA Play-Off Tournament.

event_overview.title: About Sen. Cassidy Supports Todd Blanche's Attorney General Confirmation
event_overview.subject: Sen. Cassidy Supports Todd Blanche's Attorney General Confirmation
event_overview.summary: This event concerns the Senate’s consideration and confirmation of Todd Blanche to lead the U.S. Department of Justice as Attorney General after President Donald Trump nominated him for the office. Sen. Bill Cassidy’s stated support was part of the Senate confirmation process, which followed a Judiciary Committee hearing and a closely divided full-Senate vote.

facts.label: Nomination
facts.value: President Trump sent Blanche’s nomination to the Senate on June 8, 2026, to serve as Attorney General.

facts.label: Senate process
facts.value: The Senate Judiciary Committee held a nomination hearing for Blanche on July 15, 2026, in Room 216 of the Hart Senate Office Building in Washington, D.C.

facts.label: Confirmation
facts.value: The Senate confirmed Blanche as Attorney General by a 50–49 vote on August 8, 2026, according to Associated Press reporting.

facts.label: Office and responsibilities
facts.value: The Attorney General heads the Department of Justice, represents the United States in legal matters, and advises the President and executive departments; the office originated with the Judiciary Act of 1789 and later became the head of the Justice Department established in 1870.

facts.label: Prior role
facts.value: Before this nomination, Blanche was the 40th Deputy Attorney General and later served as Acting Attorney General; the Deputy Attorney General assists in directing Justice Department policy and operations and acts as Attorney General when that office is vacant.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers Cassidy’s support and the final confirmation developments on August 7–8, 2026, rather than every hearing exchange, endorsement, objection, or Justice Department action connected to the nomination.

event_overview.title: About New Restraining Order Filed Against GOP Rep. Max Miller Amid Abuse Allegations
event_overview.subject: New Restraining Order Filed Against GOP Rep. Max Miller Amid Abuse Allegations
event_overview.summary: This event concerns a public and legal dispute involving Rep. Max Miller, an Ohio Republican, and his former wife, Emily Moreno, over domestic-abuse allegations, child-custody litigation, and related civil claims. Miller has denied abusing Moreno or their child and has separately sued Moreno and her lawyers for defamation; the allegations had also prompted a House Ethics Committee investigation as of August 5, 2026.

facts.label: People and office
facts.value: Max L. Miller is the Republican U.S. representative for Ohio’s 7th Congressional District; Emily Moreno is his former spouse and the daughter of Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno.

facts.label: Underlying litigation
facts.value: The dispute has unfolded alongside litigation over custody of Miller and Moreno’s minor child. On May 13, 2026, Miller filed a Cuyahoga County civil defamation case against Moreno and her attorneys, alleging that abuse accusations were false and damaging; the filing identifies the case as CV 26 138810 and seeks damages exceeding $25,000.

facts.label: Relevant Ohio legal framework
facts.value: Ohio Revised Code §3113.31 permits domestic-violence civil-protection-order petitions by qualifying family, household, or dating-relationship parties. It allows same-day ex parte hearings when requested and permits temporary restrictions or other relief when the court finds good cause, but proceedings do not replace other civil or criminal remedies.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the late-July to August 5, 2026 escalation—an attorney-contact restraining-order request, Bernie Moreno’s public criticism, and House Ethics action—but does not resolve the underlying allegations, custody proceedings, or defamation case.

facts.label: Initial casualties
facts.value: Russian officials initially reported at least three deaths, including the woman described in reporting as the bomber, and at least 21 people wounded.

facts.label: Method reported
facts.value: Reporting cited Russian accounts that an explosive device was detonated at the restaurant; one account said a suspicious package carried by a woman posing as a delivery worker was remotely activated.

facts.label: Official characterization
facts.value: Moscow's mayor described the incident as a terrorist act. Russian authorities and officials subsequently made allegations about responsibility, but those claims had not been independently established in the reporting consulted.

facts.label: Casualty-count uncertainty
facts.value: By August 3, reporting said the death toll had risen to five and noted that the National Anti-Terrorism Committee had initially issued a lower figure, underscoring that casualty reporting was still evolving.
