event_overview.title: About Youth Protests
event_overview.subject: Youth Protests
event_overview.summary: Youth-led demonstrations in India grew around alleged irregularities in the 2026 National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test for undergraduate medical education (NEET-UG), including claims of a leaked paper and the disruption caused by a nationwide re-examination. The protests, centered visibly in New Delhi but supported more broadly, expanded into demands for accountability, examination-system reforms, and the education minister’s departure.

facts.label: Examination and re-test dates
facts.value: NTA scheduled NEET-UG 2026 for May 3, 2026; its official notices show that a re-examination was conducted on June 21, 2026.

facts.label: Examination purpose
facts.value: NEET-UG is the common, uniform entrance test for undergraduate medical education in India; it also applies to specified undergraduate Indian-system-of-medicine and homeopathy courses.

facts.label: Exam administrator
facts.value: The National Testing Agency (NTA), an autonomous organization under India’s Ministry of Education’s Department of Higher Education, administers NEET-UG and other national entrance examinations.

facts.label: Protest setting and stated demands
facts.value: The movement’s most visible sit-in site was Jantar Mantar in central New Delhi. Organizers sought the education minister’s resignation, examination reforms, and compensation for families of students reported to have died by suicide after exam irregularities.

facts.label: Legal context
facts.value: India’s Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, in force from June 21, 2024, covers paper or answer-key leaks and related collusion among prohibited unfair means in covered public examinations.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline focuses on the youth mobilization and ministerial-resignation developments of July 25, 2026, rather than providing a complete account of the NEET investigation, re-examination administration, court process, or all related education-policy disputes.

event_overview.title: About Japan Earthquake

event_overview.summary: A magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck the Kumamoto area of Kyushu, southwestern Japan, on July 28, 2026, causing fatalities, injuries and structural damage. The disaster response includes searches for people affected by collapses and monitoring of continued seismic activity, while authorities assess localized tsunami risk and issue public warnings as needed.

facts.label: Date and location
facts.value: The main earthquake occurred on July 28, 2026, in the Kumamoto area of Kyushu, Japan’s southwestern main island.

facts.label: Magnitude and impacts
facts.value: Initial reporting described the earthquake as magnitude 7.1, with destructive shaking that damaged buildings and infrastructure and led to casualties.

facts.label: Earthquake and tsunami authority
facts.value: Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) is the national authority that rapidly determines an earthquake’s location, magnitude and observed intensity, and distributes earthquake information to disaster-prevention authorities and the public.

facts.label: Tsunami alerts
facts.value: When a quake may produce damaging coastal waves, JMA issues tsunami warnings or advisories by forecast region, generally within about two to three minutes; advisories call for people to leave the water and coast until they are lifted.

facts.label: Seismic-intensity system
facts.value: Japan reports local shaking separately from magnitude using JMA’s 10-level seismic-intensity scale, which reflects ground motion at a particular place and can vary with distance and local geology.

event_overview.scope_note: This timeline follows the July 28–29, 2026 Kumamoto-area earthquake, including rescue operations, aftershocks and tsunami alerts; it does not attempt to cover all earthquakes in Japan or every subsequent damage assessment and emergency update.

event_overview.title: About Russia Sanctions
event_overview.subject: Russia Sanctions
event_overview.summary: This event concerns the U.S. Senate’s August 7, 2026 passage of bipartisan legislation aimed at increasing economic pressure on Russia and on major foreign purchasers of Russian oil and gas, in the context of Russia’s war against Ukraine. The package also continued U.S. statutory sanctions authority affecting Iran’s energy and weapons sectors; Senate passage did not by itself make the measure law, which would also require House approval and presidential action.

facts.label: Senate action
facts.value: The Senate passed the Russia- and Iran-related sanctions package on August 7, 2026, by an 86–11 vote.

facts.label: Legislative origins
facts.value: The underlying Sanctioning Russia Act was introduced in the Senate as S. 1241 on April 1, 2025, with broad bipartisan sponsorship; the 2026 package followed negotiations to revise and advance Russia sanctions legislation.

facts.label: Russia-related scope
facts.value: The legislation is designed to authorize or require primary and secondary measures against Russian government-linked actors and those supporting Russia’s war, including Russian financial institutions, energy-related entities, the so-called shadow fleet, and specified foreign purchasers or enablers of Russian oil and gas.

facts.label: Foreign purchasers and tariffs
facts.value: The negotiated version allows targeted tariffs on imports from countries identified as among the largest buyers of Russian crude oil or gas, or among the leading countries facilitating evasion of Russia energy sanctions.

facts.label: Iran-related provision
facts.value: The package includes a provision intended to prevent the expiration of sanctions authority restricting financing for Iran’s energy and weapons sectors, alongside the Russia-focused measures.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the Senate’s August 7, 2026 approval and its Russia- and Iran-related provisions, not subsequent House consideration, enactment, executive implementation, or later sanctions designations.

event_overview.title: About Crime Extradition
event_overview.subject: Crime Extradition
event_overview.summary: This event concerns the transfer of Irish national Daniel Kinahan from the United Arab Emirates to Ireland under the two countries’ extradition framework, so that he can face criminal proceedings in Ireland. Reporting on the transfer said he was expected to appear before Ireland’s Special Criminal Court on an allegation of directing an organized crime group; the allegation remains to be determined through the Irish judicial process.

facts.label: Extradition framework
facts.value: Ireland and the UAE concluded their bilateral extradition treaty in Abu Dhabi on October 21, 2024. Ireland’s Extradition (United Arab Emirates) Order 2025 brought the UAE within Part II of Ireland’s Extradition Act 1965 from May 18, 2025.

facts.label: Legal scope
facts.value: Under the treaty, either state may seek a person for prosecution, trial, or execution of a sentence. For a prosecution request, the conduct must be punishable in both states by at least one year of imprisonment.

facts.label: Responsible authorities
facts.value: The treaty names Ireland’s Minister for Justice, or departmental officials exercising the minister’s functions, as Ireland’s central authority; the UAE Ministry of Justice is the UAE central authority.

facts.label: Broader enforcement context
facts.value: In April 2022, the U.S. Treasury Department designated the Kinahan Organized Crime Group and Daniel Kinahan under its transnational-crime sanctions authority; sanctions are an administrative measure and separate from the Irish criminal case.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the reported August 9–10, 2026 transfer and initial Irish charging stage, not the full history of the Kinahan group, the UAE court process, or the eventual outcome of any Irish prosecution.

event_overview.title: About Epstein Investigation
event_overview.subject: Epstein Investigation
event_overview.summary: The Epstein investigation refers to the overlapping U.S. criminal investigations, prosecutions, custody review, and later records-disclosure efforts concerning Jeffrey Epstein’s sexual exploitation and trafficking of minors, as well as alleged assistance by associates. It includes the 2019 federal case in New York, which ended after Epstein’s death, related proceedings involving Ghislaine Maxwell, and continuing disputes over access to Justice Department records.

facts.label: Federal criminal case
facts.value: A federal grand jury in the Southern District of New York returned an indictment in July 2019 charging Epstein with sex trafficking of minors and conspiracy to commit sex trafficking of minors; the alleged conduct covered 2002 through 2005 and included New York and Florida.

facts.label: Case outcome and continuing investigativ
facts.value: Epstein died in federal custody on August 10, 2019. The Southern District of New York formally dismissed the federal case on August 29, 2019, while stating that its investigation into his conduct continued.

facts.label: Custody review
facts.value: The Justice Department inspector general’s 2023 review focused on Bureau of Prisons personnel and identified serious failures at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York; it reported that Epstein died by suicide while in BOP custody.

facts.label: Related prosecution
facts.value: Ghislaine Maxwell, described by the Southern District of New York as Epstein’s longtime partner and co-conspirator, was convicted by a unanimous federal jury on December 29, 2021 for facilitating and participating in the sexual abuse of children.

facts.label: Records-disclosure framework
facts.value: The Epstein Files Transparency Act became Public Law 119-38 on November 19, 2025. It directs the Attorney General to publish unclassified DOJ records relating to Epstein, Maxwell, associated investigations, custodial matters, and specified related records, subject to protections including for victim-identifying information and child sexual-abuse material.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows notable later developments tied to people associated with Epstein and to access to federal investigative records; it does not attempt to catalog every allegation, civil case, prosecution, document release, or individual mentioned in the files.

event_overview.title: About Berlin Pride Attack
event_overview.subject: Berlin Pride Attack
event_overview.summary: The Berlin Pride attack refers to a deadly assault in the Tiergarten area of central Berlin on July 25, 2026, during the city’s Christopher Street Day (CSD) weekend. Berlin prosecutors said the suspected attacker allegedly used a rented vehicle and a bladed weapon against people near the event; one woman died and multiple people were injured, with the investigation continuing.

facts.label: Date and location
facts.value: Authorities place the attack at about 10 p.m. on July 25, 2026, in the Tiergarten area of Berlin, in the vicinity of Christopher Street Day celebrations.

facts.label: Alleged method and casualties
facts.value: The Berlin General Prosecutor’s Office said the suspect was alleged to have injured several people with a rented vehicle and a bladed weapon; a woman died that evening and other people were seriously injured.

facts.label: Underlying event
facts.value: Berlin CSD 2026 was the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day, organized by Berliner CSD e.V.; organizers described it as a demonstration for democracy, diversity and human rights.

facts.label: CSD schedule and format
facts.value: The Pride weekend was scheduled for July 24-25, 2026. Its July 25 demonstration was to begin on Leipziger Straße, proceed via Potsdamer Platz and Nollendorfplatz toward the Victory Column, with programming around the Brandenburg Gate.

facts.label: Investigation
facts.value: The Berlin General Prosecutor’s Office and police described the case as an active investigation and said that detailed public disclosures were limited in order to protect it.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the immediate attack and law-enforcement response on July 26-27, 2026; it does not provide a full account of the broader Berlin CSD program, later legal proceedings, or longer-term security and policy consequences.

event_overview.subject: Child Safety
event_overview.summary: This event concerns New Mexico’s civil case against Meta Platforms over alleged child-safety failures on Facebook, Instagram and related services. A jury found Meta liable under the state Unfair Practices Act in March 2026, and a subsequent court phase considered monetary and injunctive remedies; the August developments concern the resulting financial sanctions and required protections.

facts.label: Legal basis
facts.value: New Mexico alleged that Meta misled consumers about platform safety and endangered children; the March jury verdict found liability on both claims under the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act.

facts.label: Key dates and phases
facts.value: The jury returned its verdict on March 24, 2026. A second, judge-decided phase seeking public-nuisance relief and operational changes began on May 4 and concluded on May 22, 2026.

facts.label: Financial remedies
facts.value: The March verdict imposed $375 million in civil penalties. The later $567 million order reported in August was additional, bringing the reported combined financial amount to $942 million.

facts.label: Stated remedial focus
facts.value: The state sought platform changes for New Mexico users under 18, including age verification, safer recommendation systems, limits on adult-minor messaging, warning labels, permanent bans for accounts involved in exploitation, and independent oversight.

event_overview.scope_note: This Muninn timeline follows the August 7–8, 2026 penalty and remedy developments in the New Mexico Meta case; it does not attempt to cover every separate lawsuit, regulatory inquiry, appeal, or broader child-online-safety policy debate involving Meta or other platforms.

event_overview.title: About DOJ Nomination
event_overview.subject: DOJ Nomination
event_overview.summary: This event is the Senate’s consideration of President Donald Trump’s nomination of Todd Blanche to be Attorney General of the United States, the Senate-confirmed head of the Department of Justice. The Senate Judiciary Committee conducts the initial hearing and committee review; its action determines whether the nomination is reported for consideration by the full Senate, which provides the required advice and consent.

facts.label: Nominee and office
facts.value: Todd Blanche was nominated to be Attorney General of the United States, replacing Pamela Bondi. At the time of the committee proceedings, he was serving as Acting Attorney General and as the 40th Deputy Attorney General.

facts.label: Legal framework
facts.value: Federal law provides that the President appoints the Attorney General with the advice and consent of the Senate; the Attorney General is the head of the Department of Justice.

facts.label: Senate process
facts.value: The Senate Judiciary Committee has jurisdiction to consider executive nominations including senior Department of Justice positions, while the full Senate ultimately acts on the nomination.

facts.label: Committee hearings
facts.value: The committee held Blanche’s nomination hearing on July 15, 2026, followed by a second day of testimony on July 16, in Room 216 of the Hart Senate Office Building in Washington, D.C.

facts.label: Department role
facts.value: The Attorney General leads the Department of Justice, represents the United States in legal matters, and provides legal advice and opinions to the President and executive-department heads when requested.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the late-July postponement and August 4 committee action on this nomination, not every hearing exchange, negotiation, or subsequent full-Senate step.

event_overview.title: About Investigation Underway Following Deadly Shooting at Idaho In-N-Out Burger
event_overview.subject: Investigation Underway Following Deadly Shooting at Idaho In-N-Out Burger
event_overview.summary: A mass shooting occurred on August 1, 2026, at an In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, Idaho, killing three people and injuring seven others. Twin Falls police identified the suspected shooter as 24-year-old Chad Williams and said he died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound; as of August 7, investigators were still working to establish a motive and had released surveillance video of the attack.

facts.label: Date and location
facts.value: The shooting took place on Saturday, August 1, 2026, at the In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, in southern Idaho.

facts.label: Casualties
facts.value: Three people were killed and seven others were injured; police said 10 people in total were shot across the restaurant area and nearby locations.

facts.label: Suspect and investigation
facts.value: Police identified the suspected shooter as Chad Williams, 24, and said he died by a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Investigators said they were confident he acted alone, while the motive remained under investigation.

facts.label: Lead agency
facts.value: The Twin Falls Police Department is the local law-enforcement agency leading public information on the case; its chief is Matthew Hicks.

facts.label: Video release
facts.value: On August 7, police released surveillance video and described the footage as part of their public account of the shooting and response.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the August 4 investigation update and the August 7 surveillance-video release, rather than providing a complete account of every victim update, investigative step, or subsequent legal development.

event_overview.title: About Michigan Senate Primary
event_overview.subject: Michigan Senate Primary
event_overview.summary: The Michigan Senate primary is the August 4, 2026 statewide nomination contest for one of Michigan’s U.S. Senate seats. It determined each major party’s nominee for the November 3 general election, when voters will choose a senator for a six-year term.

facts.label: Primary date and jurisdiction
facts.value: The statewide primary election was held in Michigan on Tuesday, August 4, 2026.

facts.label: Office at stake
facts.value: The ballot included one statewide U.S. Senate position with a six-year term; each state has two U.S. senators.

facts.label: Democratic primary field
facts.value: Michigan’s official candidate listing named Abdul El-Sayed, Mallory McMorrow, and Haley Stevens as Democratic candidates for U.S. Senate.

facts.label: Republican primary field
facts.value: Michigan’s official candidate listing named Mike Rogers as the Republican U.S. Senate candidate; Bernadette Smith was listed as disqualified.

facts.label: Election format and next stage
facts.value: Michigan’s August primary is for eligible Democratic and Republican candidates, and the winning nominees advance to the November general-election ballot. The 2026 general election is scheduled for November 3.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the Democratic nomination contest and its immediate vote-counting developments, not the full set of Michigan primary races, the Republican nomination process, or the November general-election campaign.

event_overview.title: About Middle East Conflict
event_overview.subject: Middle East Conflict
event_overview.summary: This event concerns the risk that attacks by Yemen’s Houthi movement (Ansar Allah) on Saudi-linked oil shipping or energy infrastructure could widen the Yemen and Red Sea security crisis and disrupt oil flows. It sits within the longer Yemen conflict, in which Houthi forces took Sana’a in 2014 and Saudi Arabia led a military coalition from 2015, alongside a separate pattern of Houthi attacks on commercial navigation in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

facts.label: Origins of the Yemen conflict
facts.value: Houthi forces captured Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, in September 2014; the UN Security Council records that they then sought in January 2015 to replace the government with a Houthi-dominated authority.

facts.label: Saudi Arabia’s role
facts.value: Saudi Arabia formed and led a coalition that began military operations in Yemen in March 2015 after Yemen’s president requested external support; the conflict subsequently included Houthi cross-border missile, drone and rocket attacks on Saudi territory.

facts.label: Relevant waterways
facts.value: The maritime dimension centers on the Red Sea, the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden—routes used by merchant vessels moving between the Suez Canal and the Indian Ocean.

facts.label: International legal and diplomatic frame
facts.value: UN Security Council Resolution 2216 (2015) demanded that the Houthis end violence, withdraw from seized areas and refrain from threats or provocations against neighboring states; Resolution 2722 (2024) demanded an immediate end to Houthi attacks on merchant and commercial vessels in the Red Sea.

facts.label: Ceasefire context
facts.value: A UN-brokered Yemen truce began on April 2, 2022 and formally expired on October 2, 2022. The UN says the overall front-line military situation remained comparatively stable afterward, while its Special Envoy continued pursuing a nationwide ceasefire and Yemeni-led political settlement.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the July 2026 escalation involving alleged Houthi attacks, oil-price concerns and related U.S.-Iran diplomacy; it does not attempt to chronicle the full Yemen war, every Red Sea incident, or all regional negotiations.

event_overview.title: About US History
event_overview.subject: US History
event_overview.summary: This event concerns a July 24, 2026 executive order directing federal officials to place temporary interpretive signage and exhibits on National Park Service-managed approaches to the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. The order follows a White House review that criticized the museum’s presentation of U.S. history; it is part of a broader administration effort, begun in 2025, to influence historical interpretation at federal sites and Smithsonian institutions.

facts.label: Date and directive
facts.value: President Donald Trump issued the order on July 24, 2026. It directs the Secretary of the Interior, through the National Park Service and in coordination with the White House Domestic Policy office, to install temporary signage along NPS-maintained public sidewalks and walkways leading to the museum.

facts.label: Stated purpose and content
facts.value: The order says the signs are to convey findings from the White House report “Saving America’s Story,” state that museum exhibits should be renovated consistently with that report, and direct visitors to resources the administration describes as accurate information about U.S. history. It also calls for temporary exhibits or signs addressing information the order characterizes as inaccurate, including the treatment of

facts.label: Location
facts.value: The affected museum is the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, on the National Mall at Constitution Avenue NW between 12th and 14th Streets in Washington, D.C.

facts.label: Institutional governance
facts.value: The Smithsonian, established by Congress in 1846, is an independent federal trust instrumentality. Its administration is vested in a Board of Regents that includes the Vice President, Chief Justice, six members of Congress, and nine citizen members; it is not an executive-branch agency.

facts.label: Broader policy context
facts.value: The July 2026 order expressly builds on Executive Order 14253 of March 27, 2025, which directed administration officials to pursue the removal of what it called improper ideology from Smithsonian properties and to work with Congress on future Smithsonian appropriations.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers this specific federal action concerning signage and related pressure on the Smithsonian’s presentation of U.S. history, not every Smithsonian exhibition decision, governance matter, or broader dispute over historical interpretation.

event_overview.title: About Brazil Elections
event_overview.subject: Brazil Elections
event_overview.summary: Brazil’s 2026 general elections will choose the country’s president and vice president alongside governors, senators, and federal and state or district legislators. The presidential contest is a nationwide direct election administered by Brazil’s Electoral Justice, with a second round if no ticket wins an absolute majority of valid votes in the first round.

facts.label: Election dates
facts.value: The first round is scheduled for October 4, 2026; a second round, where required, is scheduled for October 25, 2026.

facts.label: Offices being elected
facts.value: Voters will elect the president and vice president, state and Federal District governors and vice governors, senators, federal deputies, and state or district deputies; two Senate seats are being contested in each state and the Federal District in this cycle.

facts.label: Electoral system for president
facts.value: The president and vice president run as a single ticket. A ticket must receive an absolute majority of valid votes to win in the first round; otherwise, the two leading tickets proceed to a runoff.

facts.label: Candidate selection and registration
facts.value: Political parties and federations may hold conventions from July 20 through August 5, 2026 to choose candidates and decide coalitions. A public campaign launch is distinct from the formal registration process; presidential and vice-presidential registration requests are decided by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE).

facts.label: Election administration
facts.value: The Superior Electoral Court’s 2026 rules govern preparation, voting, vote counting, tabulation, certification of winners, and post-election procedures for the general election.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows specific developments involving a presidential campaign and Brazil–Argentina diplomatic tensions, rather than providing a complete record of candidates, court rulings, polling, campaign activity, or election results.

event_overview.title: About US Primaries
event_overview.subject: US Primaries
event_overview.summary: U.S. primaries are state-administered elections held before the November general election to select or narrow the field of candidates for public office. The August 4, 2026 contests are part of the midterm-election cycle, but their rules and ballot formats differ by state.

facts.label: Date and states
facts.value: Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, Washington and Virginia hold 2026 primary elections on August 4; Arizona's 2026 primary was held earlier, on July 21.

facts.label: General-election link
facts.value: The candidates or finalists emerging from these contests proceed toward the November 3, 2026 general election, subject to each state's ballot-access and election rules.

facts.label: State-specific formats
facts.value: Primary systems are not uniform: Missouri voters may choose a party ballot, while Washington uses a top-two primary in which the two highest vote-getters for an office advance regardless of party preference.

facts.label: Administration and certification
facts.value: Election administration is decentralized through state and local election authorities; for example, Washington counties canvass August-primary results before statewide certification, while Michigan publishes its own election calendar and results through the Secretary of State.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline focuses on notable August 4 primary developments and selected high-profile races across five states, not a complete record of every primary contest, local ballot measure, result, recount, or U.S. election event.

facts.label: Hungarian Grand Prix
